Week 5 · Module 6 · five days · about 6 hours in total

Your documents will never all fit in the window. Here is how an assistant finds the right paragraph anyway.

Last week you learned to pack a context window well. This week the documents are too big to pack at all: a thousand pages of policies, contracts and tickets. The answer is to turn meaning into numbers, store those numbers, and pull out only the three paragraphs a question needs. I have cut the week into five days, from 45 minutes to a little over two hours for the lab. By the end you will have built a retrieval assistant that answers with sources, and measured how often it finds the right chunk.

Day 1 · about 45 minutes

Meaning as a place on a map

Today I want you to feel one idea in your hands: a sentence can be turned into a list of numbers, and sentences that mean the same thing get similar numbers. By the end you can explain why a search for "cab" finds a rule written about "taxis", and you will know, roughly, where those numbers come from. Both visuals are live, and so is the map above.

0.00
Similarity (1 = same meaning)0 shared words

Pick any two of the 40 questions from the map above.Scores are illustrative, from the 3D distance.

Why does the policy search miss "cab" when the rule says "taxi"?

Picture the search box on your company intranet. A colleague types "is an airport cab reimbursable" and gets nothing useful, because the expense policy says "taxis are reimbursed for airport transfers". Not one word in common. Keyword search compares spelling, and spelling is a poor proxy for meaning. Every support team, legal team and HR inbox has a version of this problem, and until recently the only fix was a list of synonyms that somebody maintained by hand.

An embedding is the fix the field settled on. An embedding model reads a piece of text and returns a vector: a list of numbers, about a thousand of them, that describes what the text is about rather than how it is spelled. "Can I claim a taxi from the airport?" and "Is a cab from the terminal reimbursable?" come out with very similar lists. "Quarterly revenue grew 12%" comes out somewhere else entirely. Compare any two sentences on the left and watch the score. The pair I have preselected shares no words at all.

The score is a cosine similarity, a measure of whether two vectors point the same way. It runs from minus one to one, and for most models a match worth acting on sits somewhere above 0.8, although the exact scale depends on the model, so you calibrate it on your own data rather than trusting a number from a blog post. The numbers on this page are illustrative. They come from the distance between points in the map above, which is itself a cartoon: a thousand-dimensional space squeezed into three so that you can look at it.

The map analogy breaks in one important way. On a real map two places are close for one reason, geography. In an embedding space closeness blends everything the model learned matters: topic, intent, tone, even the kind of document the sentence usually appears in. That is why "Charged twice this month" and "Why was I billed early?" sit together although one is a complaint and the other a question. Useful most of the time, occasionally surprising, and we meet the surprises on Day 4.

Claude does not make embeddings. They come from a separate, much smaller model trained for exactly this job. Anthropic points people to Voyage AI; n8n has embedding nodes for several providers. Keep the two models apart in your head: one turns text into coordinates, the other writes the answer.

An embedding is a list of numbers that captures what a text is about. Vector search compares those numbers, so it finds meaning, not spelling.

A cartoon of an embedding model. The real inner layer has 1,024 or more numbers, not eight.MIT xPRO, Module 3

Where do the numbers come from?

In Week 1 you watched a ticket sorter learn. Every ticket passed through layers of simple units, and thousands of weights shifted until the final layer said "billing" or "technical". The MIT xPRO course, in its module on neural networks, points out something easy to miss in that picture: the layer just before the answer is already a description of the ticket. Its units light up in a pattern that captures what the ticket is about, because that is the only way the last layer can get the answer right. Read those activations off as a list of numbers and you have an embedding.

The MIT instructors show this with an autoencoder, a network trained to squeeze an input down to a few numbers and then rebuild it. Trained on images of handwritten digits, 256 pixel values in and 256 out, with only two numbers allowed in the middle, the network had no choice but to make those two numbers mean something. Plotted on a page, the zeros, ones and twos fell into separate groups, and nobody had told it what a two looks like. Modern embedding models do the same with text, at a scale of a thousand numbers rather than two, trained on millions of pairs of texts that people agreed were about the same thing.

Pick a sentence on the left and watch it travel. Tokens go in, the layers do their arithmetic, and the inner layer settles into a pattern. I have drawn eight units; a real model has a thousand or more, and the plot on the right uses two of them as coordinates. The two taxi sentences land close together. The revenue sentence does not.

This is also why embedding models are cheap to run. They are small compared with Claude, they read the text once, and they return the numbers in a few milliseconds for a fraction of a cent. You can afford to embed every paragraph of every policy your company has written, which is exactly what we will do on Day 5.

An embedding is a neural network's inner layer read off as coordinates. The network learned to place similar texts together because that was the only way to do its job.

Day 2 · about 55 minutes

Groups without labels, and documents cut to size

Two ideas that explain most of the retrieval quality you will ever get. First, why similar things sit together even when nobody labelled them, an idea the MIT course teaches as clustering. Then chunking: how to cut a long document so each piece means one thing. By the end you will have chunked a policy by hand and watched three chunk sizes succeed or fail on the same question.

unsorted · hover a dot
Nobody labelled these tickets. The algorithm only knows distances.MIT xPRO, Module 2

Nobody labelled these tickets. Why do they still form groups?

Export a month of support tickets with no tags, no categories, nothing but the text. Most managers assume you would have to read them to find the themes. You do not. The MIT xPRO course calls this unsupervised learning: there are inputs but no labels, and the job is to find structure in the data itself. Clustering is its simplest form, and the k-means algorithm the MIT instructors walk through is almost embarrassingly plain.

Press Find the groups. The algorithm starts with k guesses, assigns every ticket to its nearest guess, moves each guess to the middle of the tickets it collected, and repeats until nothing changes. Four or five rounds is usually enough. Hover any dot to read the ticket. The groups that appear are billing, shipping, login and leave, and no one typed those words into the machine. They emerged because similar tickets had similar coordinates.

Here is why this matters for retrieval. The embedding model places similar texts together for the same reason the clusters form: it had to, in order to do its training job. So when a question arrives, the chunks that answer it are already sitting in its neighbourhood, and "retrieve" means nothing more than "look around". The MIT course also warns about the catch: k is a choice you make before you start. Slide k to six and watch the algorithm invent groups that are not really there. Retrieval has the same knob, called top-k, and we spend most of Day 4 on it.

A trick worth stealing from the MIT course. When labelling is expensive, cluster first, label one example per cluster by hand, and let the label spread to the rest of the cluster. A support lead can tag four tickets instead of four hundred.

Similar texts get similar coordinates, so they form groups nobody labelled. Retrieval is looking around a question's neighbourhood.

Question: Can I claim a taxi from the airport? Teal outline: the taxi rule sits whole in that chunk. Dashed red: cut in half.0 chunks

How do you cut a 40-page policy so each piece means one thing?

You cannot embed the whole expense policy as a single vector. The model would average six topics into one list of numbers that is about nothing in particular, and a question about taxis would match it weakly. So you split the document into chunks, embed each chunk, and let a question find the chunk that answers it. How you split matters more than people expect, and it is the knob you will turn most often in the lab.

Try the sizes on the left. At 100 tokens the taxi rule is cut in half and the half about receipts lands in a different chunk; retrieval may return one half and the answer will be incomplete. At 2,000 tokens one chunk holds the whole policy and we are back to the blurred vector, with the prompt full of meals and laptops. Between 300 and 800 tokens the rule sits whole, next to the receipt cap that belongs with it. That range is a starting point, not a law: dense legal text wants smaller chunks, narrative handbooks tolerate larger ones.

Two strategies beat fixed sizes when you can use them. Split at section headings, so a chunk is a section and carries its own title; switch the toggle to see the policy cut that way. Or split by paragraph when there are no headings. And whatever you do, never cut a table in half: a row without its header means nothing to the model, or to the person who later follows the citation. Overlap, a few sentences repeated at each boundary, is cheap insurance against a sentence split across two chunks.

This is what the syllabus means by dynamic chunking: the strategy adapts to the document. A contract, a spreadsheet export and a chat log should not be cut the same way, and the only way to know your choice works is to test it, which is Day 5.

Chunk so each piece means one thing and carries its context. Start at 300 to 800 tokens, split at headings when you can, never cut a table, and test before you trust.

2. Approval. Any expense over 100 units needs written approval from your manager before you spend it.
3. Travel. Use public transport where it is available and reasonable. Taxis are reimbursed for airport

Day 3 · about 60 minutes

The store, the search and the loop

Today the pieces become a system. A vector store answers one question very fast, semantic search beats the keyword search you have used for twenty years, and the full RAG loop ties ingest and answer together. By the end you can draw the loop on a whiteboard, you will have made Claude act as a toy vector store, and your real store will be ready for Day 5.

Each stored vector keeps its text and metadata: doc_name, section, chunk_id, last_updated.

A database built for one question: which stored vectors are closest to this one?

Your company already runs databases that answer "which rows match this filter" in milliseconds. A vector store is a database built for a different question: given a new vector, which of the million vectors I hold are nearest to it? Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector inside Postgres, and n8n's In-Memory Vector Store all do this. They differ in price, hosting and how many vectors they hold before they slow down, not in the question they answer.

Each record in the store holds three things: the vector, the original text of the chunk, and metadata such as doc_name, section, chunk_id and the date it was indexed. The vector is for finding. The text is what you hand to Claude. The metadata is what becomes the citation. Watch the search run on the left: the question is embedded, compared with every stored vector, and the five closest light up with their ids.

The comparison looks expensive, and at a million vectors a naive version would be. Real stores use index structures that find near neighbours without checking every vector, trading a little accuracy for a lot of speed. The MIT xPRO course describes the ancestor of this idea under the name nearest neighbours: a table of everything you have seen, and a lookup for the closest entry. The index just makes the lookup fast.

One honest limit. A store returns the nearest vectors whether or not they are any good. Ask about parental leave with only an expense policy loaded and you still get five results, ranked by similarity, every one of them irrelevant. The store does not know what "relevant" means. That is why we ask for the similarity score alongside each result, and why Day 4 is about failures.

A vector store holds vector, text and metadata for every chunk and returns the nearest few to a question. The metadata becomes your citation.

Keyword search · top 3
Semantic search · top 3
Ten chunks from the policy set. Green border: the chunk that actually answers the question. Highlighted words: exact matches.Simplified engines; real keyword search also stems words.

Keyword search versus semantic search, on the same five questions

You have used keyword search since your first job: type words, get the documents that contain those words, ranked by how often they appear. It is fast, cheap and transparent, and it fails in a predictable way. The person asking and the person who wrote the document chose different words. Pick a question on the left and compare the two columns. The chunk that actually answers it has a green border.

Semantic search embeds the question, finds the nearest chunks, and does not care how anything is spelled. "Cab from the terminal" finds the taxi rule. "Days off a year" finds the leave entitlement instead of the expense deadline that happens to contain the word "days". "Working from Spain for a month" finds the remote-work rule although Spain appears nowhere in the documents. This is what the syllabus means by semantic retrieval, and it is the reason the whole week exists.

Keyword search is not useless, and I want to be fair to it. When the question uses the document's own vocabulary, a form name, a part number, a person's name, exact matching is better than meaning: an embedding model may treat "form 27B" and "form 27C" as near twins. Production systems often run both and merge the results, which the field calls hybrid search. For the lab, semantic alone is enough. For your product, keep hybrid in mind wherever names and codes matter.

Semantic search matches meaning, keyword search matches spelling. Meaning wins for questions in plain words, spelling wins for codes and names, and many systems use both.

Press Play to walk through both phases.
Seven steps. Claude enters at the last one.RAG · retrieval-augmented generation

The full loop: ingest once, then answer every question

Put the pieces in order and you have retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, the pattern inside nearly every serious enterprise assistant. There are two phases and they run at different times. Ingest happens once, or whenever a document changes: split into chunks, embed each chunk, store vector plus text plus metadata. Answering happens on every question: embed the question, retrieve the top chunks, build a prompt that puts those chunks inside <context> tags, and ask Claude to answer only from them and to cite the chunk each fact came from.

Press Play on the left and read each step. Notice how little Claude does. It never searches, never reads the store, never sees the documents that were not retrieved. It sees five chunks and a question. Everything you learned in Week 4 about packing a context window still applies, except that now a machine does the packing, one question at a time.

Do you always need this? No. If the whole corpus is under fifty pages, a Claude Project from Week 3 keeps it on the desk permanently and you skip the store entirely. RAG earns its complexity when the documents will not fit, change often, or need per-user access control so that one team's contracts never reach another's questions. Choosing between "paste it", "Project" and "RAG" is a design decision, and it is the first question in this week's design-log entry.

Where it breaks. Retrieval runs before the model reads anything, so a question whose answer is spread across a whole document, "summarise this policy", gets five chunks and a partial summary delivered with confidence. RAG is a lookup pattern. For whole-document work, Week 4's techniques are still the right tool.

Ingest once: chunk, embed, store. Per question: embed, retrieve, build <context>, answer with citations. Claude only ever sees the retrieved chunks.

Day 4 · about 70 minutes

Sources you can check, and the ways retrieval fails

Citations turn "the AI said so" into "section 3 of the expense policy says so". Today you learn how a citation is tracked from the store to the sentence, how to verify one, and the five ways a RAG pipeline produces a wrong answer with a perfectly good model. By the end you will have written the five test questions you will use in the lab.

    3 citations · unchecked
    Click a citation to light up its chunk. Then check them against the context.citation tracking

    How does a sentence know which chunk it came from?

    A finance lead asks the assistant whether airport taxis are claimable and gets a confident yes. Before she acts on it she wants one thing: where does it say that? In Week 1 you learned that a model's confidence tells you nothing about its correctness. Citations are the fix, and they are mechanical rather than clever. Every chunk arrives in the prompt with its chunk_id, the system prompt tells Claude to write [source: chunk_id] after every factual sentence, and the metadata the store returned turns that id into "Expense policy, section 3, Travel".

    Read the answer on the left. Three sentences, three citations. Click one and its chunk lights up in the context. Now press Check citations. Two are real. The third points at expenses-09, a chunk that was never retrieved: the model wrote a plausible-looking id. That is the Week 1 invented fact wearing a citation, and it is why a program, not a person, should verify every id against the context before the answer reaches a user.

    The verifier is twenty lines of code, or a Code node in n8n. Pull every [source: ...] out of the answer, check each against the list of ids you put into the context, and flag or strip the ones that do not match. Go one step further and check that the cited chunk actually contains a sentence close to the claim; that catches the subtler failure, a real id attached to the wrong fact.

    Then show the sources the way a person wants them. Press "As the user sees it": footnotes with the document name, the section and the date it was indexed, each one a link to the original. Most of the trust your assistant earns comes from this screen, not from the model.

    A citation is a chunk_id that travels from the store, through the prompt, into the answer. Verify every id against the context before anyone reads the answer.

    Five ways to get a wrong answer with a perfectly good model

    When a RAG assistant answers badly, almost everyone blames the model. In my experience the model is the last place to look. Walk through the five failure modes on the left. The orange squares are the chunks that hold the answer; the teal ones are what you actually handed to Claude.

    Not retrieved: the right chunk never appears at any rank, usually because it was cut mid-sentence or the question was vague. Ranked sixth: the chunk exists but sits just outside your top five, so Claude never sees it. Needs two chunks: the taxi rule is at rank two and the receipt cap at rank seven, so you get half an answer delivered with full confidence. Stale index: the policy changed in March and nobody re-ran the ingest, so retrieval works perfectly and quotes a rule that no longer exists, citation and all. Too many results: k is ten, six of the ten are about meals and laptops, and they compete for the model's attention until the meal allowance leaks into the taxi answer.

    Each has its own fix, and none of them is "a bigger model". Better chunks or a rewritten question. A larger k, raised only as far as needed, because every chunk costs tokens and attention. Splitting a two-part question into two retrievals. Re-embedding on a schedule and storing last_updated so the date shows beside the source. A similarity threshold or a re-ranker that drops weak matches before they reach the prompt.

    The debugging habit. Log what was retrieved for every question: ids and scores. When an answer is wrong, read that log before you touch the prompt or the model. Nine times out of ten the problem is visible there.

    When the answer is wrong, look at what was retrieved. Wrong chunk, too few, missing context, stale index, too many: each has a fix, and none is "a bigger model".

    Day 5 · about 130 minutes

    Measure it, then build it

    The long day. One idea first, borrowed from the MIT course: you do not know retrieval is good until you measure it on questions with known answers. Then Lab 2.2, where you build the retrieval assistant, score it at three chunk sizes, verify its citations and write design-log entry 5. The quiz and a practice round close the week.

    Eight test questions, three chunk sizes · top-k = 5
    Test question100 tok300 tok2,000 tok

    Rank of the chunk that answers each question. Green: inside the top k. A dash: never retrieved.MIT xPRO, Module 2

    How do you know retrieval is good? Measure it on questions you wrote first

    In Week 1 you heard the MIT xPRO course insist on a held-out test set: keep some examples back, never train on them, and judge the model on those alone. Retrieval needs exactly the same discipline, and almost nobody applies it. The usual way people judge a RAG assistant is to ask it a few questions, feel reassured by the fluent answers, and ship. You now know that fluent answers prove nothing.

    The metric that matters is simple. For each test question, at what rank did the chunk that actually answers it appear? From that you get hit rate at k: the share of questions where the right chunk is inside the top k. Slide k on the left. At k = 5 the 300-token chunks find seven of eight and the 2,000-token chunks find four. Raise k to ten and the gap narrows, because a big enough net catches almost everything, but look at the token count underneath. You are now sending Claude twenty thousand tokens per question to hide a chunking problem.

    Eight questions is a toy. The lab asks for five because you are one person with an afternoon. A team shipping a real assistant wants fifty to a hundred, written by the people who will use it, kept away from whoever tunes the system, and re-run every time the chunking, the embedding model or the documents change. Treat the scorecard you fill in below as the first page of that test set.

    Decide the right chunk for each test question before you search, then measure hit rate at k. Raising k can hide a chunking problem, and the token count shows the price.

    A retrieval assistant with citation tracking

      Which embedding model?

      Not Claude; Claude writes the answers. Any provider works (Voyage AI, OpenAI, Cohere, Google), but whichever you choose for ingest you must also use for the questions. Vectors from two different models do not compare, so a question embedded with one and chunks embedded with another returns nonsense that looks like results.

      The Workbench is at console.anthropic.com. Put the system prompt in the System field, the context and question in the user message. A citation is wrong if its id is not in your context, or if the chunk with that id does not say what the sentence claims. Both count as failures on the scorecard.

    7. Ask one question your documents do not cover. The assistant should say "The documents do not cover this" and stop. If it answers anyway, tighten the prompt until it does, and keep the final wording.

    8. Break it on purpose. Re-chunk one document into 2,000-token pieces, re-embed, re-run the five questions and fill the second column. Then 100-token pieces, third column. Watch which column wins and where each one fails.

      Stuck? Show a hint

      In n8n, change the splitter's chunk size and run the ingest again into a fresh store. On Qdrant, make a second and third collection, one per size, so you can compare them side by side instead of overwriting.

    9. Verify three answers, tick the three boxes below, and write design-log entry 5.

    Check yourself

    Eight quick questions

    Pick an answer to see why it is right or wrong. Score 80 percent or more to pass. Nobody is watching; the point is to find out what did not stick.

    Think it through

    Why does vector search find "I forgot my login" when the document says "password reset"?

    The embedding model was trained on enormous amounts of text in which those two phrases appear in the same situations: the same help pages, the same tickets, the same replies. It learned to place them at nearby points, and the search compares points, not words. Nothing in the pipeline ever matched a spelling. That is also the weakness: two phrases that look alike to the model but differ in one crucial code or number can land closer than they should, which is why hybrid search exists.

    What is the trade-off between tiny chunks and huge chunks?

    Tiny chunks are precise but cut rules away from their exceptions and lose the context that makes a sentence mean something, so you retrieve half an answer. Huge chunks keep the context but blur six topics into one vector that matches everything weakly, and they fill the prompt with text the question did not need. Somewhere between 300 and 800 tokens, split at headings, usually wins, but the honest answer is that you test three sizes on a held-out set of questions and let the scorecard decide.

    The assistant answers confidently with no citation. What probably went wrong in the pipeline?

    Either nothing relevant was retrieved and the model fell back on prediction, exactly the Week 1 invented fact, or the system prompt never required a citation, or it required one and nobody verified the output, so a missing citation slipped through. Check the retrieval log first: were the right ids there? If not, fix chunking or the question. If they were, tighten the prompt and add the verifier that rejects any answer with an uncited factual sentence.

    Your scorecard shows five out of five at 300 tokens. A colleague says "ship it". What would the MIT course say?

    Five questions is a very small test set, and if you wrote them after seeing what the store returned, they are not held out at all; they are the training set. The MIT course would ask for questions written by the people who will use the assistant, kept away from whoever tuned it, and enough of them that one lucky hit does not move the score by twenty points. It would also ask what happens when the documents change next month, because a scorecard measures today's index. Ship a pilot, keep measuring, and grow the set.
